# Exact positive-normal reduction for common-vertex simplex fibers

Let
\[
T_d=\{X\in\mathbb R^d:X_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^dX_i\le1\},
\qquad d\ge1.
\]
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be finite, \(r_p>0\), and let the source be the sum of ordinary \(d\)-volume on the fibers \(\{p\}\times r_pT_d\). Fix \(j\in P\), and put
\[
q=\frac{r_j}{d+1},\qquad y_j=q(1,\ldots,1).
\]
Assume there is an affine majorant of the sampled radii touching at \(j\):
\[
r_p\le\ell_j(p)=r_j+b\cdot(p-j)\qquad(p\in P).
\tag{1}
\]

Then the absolute depth at the actual own-fiber centroid has the exact formula
\[
\boxed{
A_\mu(j,y_j)=
\min_{\substack{w_i\ge0,\ \sum_iw_i=1\\a\in\mathbb R^n}}
\ \sum_{p\in P}
\left|r_pT_d\cap
\{X:a\cdot(p-j)+w\cdot X\ge q\}\right|.
}
\tag{2}
\]
The minimum is attained, and the tilt \(a\) can be restricted to an explicitly bounded set depending only on \(P,j\), and the radii, as shown below.

More strongly, every ambient closed cap containing \((j,y_j)\) has a cap of the form in (2) with **no larger mass on any individual source fiber**. The reduction does not permit independent integer tilts on different fibers.

If \(P\subset\mathbb Z^n\) and the fibers are those of an actual convex body, condition (1) follows from actual convexity; see Section 3. Thus the result applies to a nested-simplex chain with any continuous concave piecewise-affine profile and integer breakpoints. No affine transformation of the base lattice, diagonal-normal hypothesis, or regularity of a minimizing cap is assumed.

## 1. A volume-preserving barycentric swap

First translate a containing cap parallel to itself until its boundary passes through \((j,y_j)\). This only decreases its mass on every fiber. Write its margin as
\[
L(p,X)=a\cdot(p-j)+\sum_{\ell=1}^du_\ell(X_\ell-q),
\tag{3}
\]
with \(H=\{L\ge0\}\). Initially suppose \(u\ne0\).

If all \(u_\ell\ge0\), the desired sign restriction already holds. Otherwise choose an index \(i\) where \(u_i=\min\{0,u_1,\ldots,u_d\}<0\).
On each fiber perform the barycentric swap
\[
(\sigma_{p,i}X)_i=r_p-\sum_{\ell=1}^dX_\ell,\qquad
(\sigma_{p,i}X)_\ell=X_\ell\quad(\ell\ne i).
\tag{4}
\]
This is an affine involution of \(r_pT_d\) with determinant \(-1\). It exchanges vertex zero and vertex \(r_pe_i\), and preserves ordinary \(d\)-volume. At the distinguished fiber it fixes \(y_j\), because \(r_j-dq=q\).

Define
\[
\widetilde u_i=-u_i,\qquad
\widetilde u_\ell=u_\ell-u_i\quad(\ell\ne i).
\tag{5}
\]
All these coefficients are nonnegative, and \(\widetilde u_i>0\).
Direct expansion, using \((d+1)q=r_j\), gives the exact identity
\[
L(p,\sigma_{p,i}X)
=a\cdot(p-j)+\widetilde u\cdot(X-y_j)+u_i(r_p-r_j).
\tag{6}
\]

Since \(u_i<0\), the majorization (1) implies
\[
u_i(r_p-r_j)\ge u_i\,b\cdot(p-j).
\]
Consequently the single **ambient affine** margin
\[
\widetilde L(p,X)
=(a+u_i b)\cdot(p-j)+\widetilde u\cdot(X-y_j)
\tag{7}
\]
satisfies \(\widetilde L(p,X)\le L(p,\sigma_{p,i}X)\) on every sampled fiber. It vanishes at \((j,y_j)\). Therefore
\[
\left|r_pT_d\cap\{\widetilde L\ge0\}\right|
\le
\left|r_pT_d\cap\{L(p,\sigma_{p,i}X)\ge0\}\right|
=\left|r_pT_d\cap\{L\ge0\}\right|
\tag{8}
\]
for every \(p\in P\).

The barycentric swaps need not be one ambient affine transformation. They are used only as exact fiberwise changes of variables; equation (7), not the swap itself, provides the genuine replacement halfspace. This distinction is essential when the roof is not affine.

Divide \((a+u_i b,\widetilde u)\) by the positive number
\(\sum_\ell\widetilde u_\ell\). The resulting continuous normal \(w\) lies in the probability simplex, and \(w\cdot y_j=q\), giving the form in (2). If the original \(u\) was already nonnegative, the same positive normalization applies directly.

## 2. Purely base-normal caps

Now suppose \(u=0\). The through-point cap is
\(\{a\cdot(p-j)\ge0\}\). For a sufficiently large positive \(R\), use
\[
R\,a\cdot(p-j)+X_1-q\ge0.
\tag{9}
\]
There are finitely many source fibers. If \(a\cdot(p-j)>0\), take \(R\) large enough that (9) contains the whole fiber. If \(a\cdot(p-j)<0\), take \(R\) large enough that it excludes the whole fiber. If \(a\cdot(p-j)=0\), its trace is an ordinary axis cap, contained in the whole fiber that the original closed base-normal cap captured.

For example, any \(R\) strictly larger than
\[
\max_{\substack{p\in P\\a\cdot(p-j)\ne0}}
\frac{q+r_p}{|a\cdot(p-j)|}
\]
works; an empty maximum imposes no condition. Thus (9) also has no larger mass on each fiber and has a positive continuous normal. This retains every original whole boundary fiber rather than treating it as null.

Together with Section 1, this proves equality of the infima over all caps and over the positive-normal class. The opposite inequality follows because the latter is a subclass of actual ambient caps.

## 3. Why an actual finite fiber family supplies the majorant

Suppose \(P\) is the set of positive fibers of an actual convex body and they are \(r_pT_d\). Any anchored convex representation \(j=\sum_p\lambda_pp\), with \(\lambda_p\ge0\) and \(\sum_p\lambda_p=1\), gives
\[
\left(\sum_p\lambda_pr_p\right)T_d
=\sum_p\lambda_p(r_pT_d)\subseteq r_jT_d.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_p\lambda_pr_p\le r_j.
\tag{10}
\]

The finite linear system for \(b\) in (1) is
\[
b\cdot(p-j)\ge r_p-r_j\qquad(p\in P).
\]
By finite Farkas separation, infeasibility would give nonnegative numbers \(\eta_p\) with
\[
\sum_p\eta_p(p-j)=0,\qquad
\sum_p\eta_p(r_p-r_j)>0.
\]
Their sum is positive. Normalize it to one; the resulting anchored representation contradicts (10). This proves (1), including at a boundary base and when \(\operatorname{aff}P\) is lower-dimensional.

Only the finite sampled majorant is used. No finite derivative or ambient supporting roof at every real base is required. In the one-dimensional piecewise-affine setting, a global majorant is available directly: choose a slope between the finite right and left slopes at an interior point, the right slope at the left endpoint, or the left slope at the right endpoint. Concavity puts the whole profile below the corresponding line.

Zero-radius fibers carry zero \(d\)-volume and may be omitted from \(P\); this is a \(d\ge1\) theorem at a positive own fiber. It asserts no discrete \(d=0\) reduction. For general common-vertex simplices, one common invertible continuous linear change of coordinates reduces to \(T_d\), multiplying all masses by the same determinant. A common vertex depending affinely on the base can first be removed by a base-preserving affine shear. Neither operation changes the original integer base.

## 4. A compact tilt interval in one base dimension

Assume \(n=1\). For \(P\ne\{j\}\), set
\[
B_j=\max_{p\in P\setminus\{j\}}
\frac{\max\{q,|q-r_p|\}}{|p-j|}.
\tag{11}
\]
For \(P=\{j\}\), set \(B_j=0\).
For every \(w\) in the probability simplex and \(X\in r_pT_d\),
\[
0\le w\cdot X\le r_p.
\tag{12}
\]
If \(a\ge B_j\), every fiber with \(p>j\) is fully captured, while every fiber with \(p<j\) has zero captured \(d\)-volume. The same holds at \(a=B_j\): an excluded trace may be a supporting face, still of zero \(d\)-volume. The own-fiber trace is independent of \(a\). Reversing signs handles \(a\le-B_j\).

Consequently clipping \(a\) to \([-B_j,B_j]\) preserves every cap mass in the positive-normal class. This is an explicit compact domain for (2). Formula (11) uses the actual base coordinates; it does not assume a translated, rescaled, or consecutively labeled lattice interval.

The objective is jointly continuous in \((a,w)\) on this domain. Indeed \(\sum_iw_i=1\) keeps the continuous normal nonzero, so its boundary has zero \(d\)-volume in each positive fiber. Dominated convergence applies to the indicator under any convergent sequence of parameters, and there are finitely many fibers. The probability simplex and tilt interval are compact, proving attainment.

## 5. A compact finite-trace replacement in arbitrary base dimension

Let \(L=\operatorname{span}\{p-j:p\in P\}\) have dimension \(m\). Components of \(a\) perpendicular to \(L\) do not affect any source cap and may be set to zero. If \(m=0\), take \(a=0\).

For \(m>0\), choose any orthonormal coordinate map \(E:\mathbb R^m\to L\), and put \(v_p=E^T(p-j)\). Set
\[
C_j=\max_{p\in P}\max\{q,|q-r_p|\}.
\]
For every set \(I\) of \(m\) independent vectors \(v_p\), let \(V_I\) be the matrix with these vectors as rows, and define the finite bound
\[
B_j^{(m)}=C_j\max_I\|V_I^{-1}\|_\infty,
\tag{13}
\]
where the matrix norm is the largest absolute row sum. These are ordinary real coordinates in the existing base span, not a change of the source lattice.

For a given tilt \(a\in L\), classify each trace \(s_p=a\cdot(p-j)\) as:

* finite if \(q-r_p\le s_p\le q\);
* full if \(s_p>q\);
* empty if \(s_p<q-r_p\).

Consider the nonempty polyhedron of replacement coordinate vectors \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
v_p\cdot b=s_p\quad\text{on finite traces},\qquad
v_p\cdot b\ge q\quad\text{on full traces},\qquad
v_p\cdot b\le q-r_p\quad\text{on empty traces}.
\tag{14}
\]
It has no line: a line direction would be orthogonal to every \(v_p\), and these span \(\mathbb R^m\). It therefore has a vertex. An elementary justification is to start at a feasible point; if active rows do not span \(\mathbb R^m\), move along a direction annihilating them. At least one of the two directions reaches a new constraint in finite distance, since otherwise the full line would be feasible. Repeating increases the rank of the active rows until it is \(m\).

At a vertex, choose \(m\) independent active rows. Their right sides all have absolute value at most \(C_j\). Equation (13) gives
\[
\|b\|_\infty\le B_j^{(m)}.
\tag{15}
\]
The tilt \(a'=Eb\) preserves each finite trace, retains each full trace, and retains zero mass on each empty trace by (12). Supporting faces newly appearing on an empty trace have zero \(d\)-volume. Thus it preserves **every positive-normal cap mass**, simultaneously for all \(w\) in the probability simplex. No hinge or first-moment preservation is asserted.

We may therefore restrict (2) to \(a=Eb\) with
\(\|b\|_\infty\le B_j^{(m)}\). The same continuity argument as in Section 4 proves attainment in arbitrary base dimension.

## 6. Scope of the reduction

The point is the **own-fiber centroid**. The barycentric swap need not fix another point of that fiber, so the theorem is not an all-candidate positive-normal reduction. Likewise positivity of the coefficients does not imply that they are all equal, or that only one is nonzero.

The exact counterexample **candidate 15438eaf9a458a13** shows that the latter restrictions are false even for three nested triangular fibers: radii \((1/2,3/2,3/4)\), the middle centroid, and one shared base tilt. A strictly unequal positive normal is cheaper than every coordinate normal and every all-equal normal after their tilts have each been optimized.

The theorem retains the full probability simplex of positive continuous coefficients, one actual shared integer tilt, every source cap mass, and all closed boundaries. It supplies a smaller exact all-cap optimization problem; it does not prove that its value reaches \(\Gamma_dM/2^n\).

In fact, an existential own-centroid selector is already false in this class when \(n=d=1\). The entry **Every fiber midpoint fails in n=d=1** in **candidate 8dd62757ee4f1859** gives the actual nested intervals \([0,2],[0,6],[0,10],[0,3]\) at bases \(0,1,2,3\), with total mass \(21\). Their four midpoints admit caps of masses \(1,5,5,3/2\), respectively, all below \(21/4\). The radii form a concave two-slope profile. Thus the reduction cannot justify selecting one of these centroids; movable points must remain available. The companion **candidate 44a12d13f3aabab3** supplies a valid reduction to a segment of movable points and retains the necessary additional roof term.

The standard-library verifier **../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_common_vertex_positive_normal_reduction.py** checks the swap identity, centroid fixation, fiberwise margin domination, positive coefficients, the one-dimensional saturation bound, and finite-trace replacement vertices in a two-dimensional example. The arguments above prove the general statements independently of these finite checks.
